Criterion A: Knowing and understanding:
# Criterion A: Knowing and understanding
## What it assesses
Criterion A: Knowing and understanding assesses mathematical knowledge in tests and exams. You select appropriate mathematics when solving problems in both familiar and unfamiliar situations; apply the selected mathematics successfully; and solve problems correctly in a variety of contexts.

## How to do well
Show all working so method marks can be given. Check that answers are reasonable. Practise a range of question types, including unfamiliar ones.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Method: the steps used to solve a problem
Familiar situation: a type of problem practised before
Working: the written steps of a solution
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion B: Investigating patterns:
# Criterion B: Investigating patterns
## What it assesses
Criterion B: Investigating patterns assesses how you explore mathematical patterns. You select and apply mathematical problem-solving techniques to discover complex patterns; describe patterns as general rules consistent with findings; and prove, or verify and justify, general rules.

## How to do well
Organize results in a table. Look for differences and ratios. Write a general rule in words and algebra. Test the rule with new cases and explain why it works.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Pattern: a regularity in numbers or shapes
General rule: a rule that works for every case
Verify: check a rule with new cases
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion C: Communicating:
# Criterion C: Communicating
## What it assesses
Criterion C: Communicating assesses how you present mathematics. You use appropriate mathematical language (notation, symbols and terminology) in both oral and written explanations; use appropriate forms of mathematical representation to present information; move between different forms of representation; communicate complete, coherent and concise lines of reasoning; and organize information using a logical structure.

## How to do well
Use correct notation and units. Label graphs and diagrams. Explain each step clearly and in a logical order.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Notation: symbols used in mathematics
Representation: a form such as a graph, table or equation
Line of reasoning: a connected chain of steps
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion D: Applying mathematics in rea:
# Criterion D: Applying mathematics in real-life contexts
## What it assesses
Criterion D: Applying mathematics in real-life contexts assesses how you use mathematics to solve real problems. You identify relevant elements of authentic real-life situations; select appropriate mathematical strategies; apply them to reach a valid solution; justify the degree of accuracy of the solution; and justify whether the solution makes sense in the context.

## How to do well
State the assumptions you make. Choose a suitable model. Round sensibly and explain the accuracy. Reflect on whether the answer is realistic.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Real-life context: an authentic situation outside mathematics
Assumption: something taken as true to simplify a problem
Degree of accuracy: how precisely an answer is given
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required

Form is the shape and underlying structure of an entity or piece of work, including its organization, essential nature and external appearance. It is one of the sixteen MYP key concepts, broad ideas that connect subjects. Number:
# Number
## The topic
Number covers forms of number, operations and their properties. Integers are whole numbers, including negatives. Rational numbers can be written as fractions; irrational numbers, such as π and √2, cannot. A prime number has exactly two factors. The highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM) are found from prime factorization. Standard form writes numbers as a × 10ⁿ. Percentages, ratios and proportion compare quantities.

## Key terms
Integer: a whole number, positive, negative or zero
Rational number: a number that can be written as a fraction
Irrational number: a number that cannot be written as a fraction
Prime number: a number with exactly two factors
Standard form: a number written as a × 10ⁿ
Ratio: a comparison of two quantities
Algebra:
# Algebra
## The topic
Algebra uses letters to represent numbers. An expression has no equals sign; an equation does. To solve an equation, do the same to both sides. Expanding removes brackets; factorising puts them in. A linear function has the form y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. Simultaneous equations are solved by substitution or elimination. Sequences can be described by an nth-term rule. Quadratic equations are solved by factorising or the quadratic formula.

## Key terms
Expression: a combination of terms with no equals sign
Equation: a statement that two expressions are equal
Gradient: the steepness of a line
Factorising: writing an expression as a product of factors
Simultaneous equations: equations solved together
nth term: a rule giving any term of a sequence
Geometry and trigonometry:
# Geometry and trigonometry
## The topic
Geometry studies shape, size and position. Angles on a straight line sum to 180° and in a triangle to 180°. Area of a triangle is ½ × base × height; area of a circle is πr²; circumference is 2πr. Pythagoras’ theorem states a² + b² = c² in a right-angled triangle. Trigonometric ratios are sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan = opposite/adjacent. Transformations include translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement. Similar shapes have the same shape but different sizes.

## Key terms
Pythagoras’ theorem: a² + b² = c² in a right-angled triangle
Hypotenuse: the longest side of a right-angled triangle
Circumference: the distance around a circle
Similar shapes: shapes with the same shape but different sizes
Transformation: a change in position or size of a shape
Trigonometric ratio: sin, cos or tan of an angle
Statistics and probability:
# Statistics and probability
## The topic
Statistics is collecting, presenting and analysing data. The mean is the total divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most common; the range is the largest minus the smallest. Graphs include bar charts, histograms, pie charts, scatter graphs and box plots. Correlation describes the relationship in a scatter graph. Probability is a number from 0 to 1 showing how likely an event is. Independent events do not affect each other.

## Key terms
Mean: the total divided by the number of values
Median: the middle value
Range: the largest value minus the smallest
Correlation: the relationship between two variables
Probability: how likely an event is, from 0 to 1
Independent events: events that do not affect each other
